notes.short: Side by side: Rahab believes, her people lose heart
notes.about: Rahab and her people hear the same news of what the LORD has done. Their hearts melt, and hers does too, but she goes on to confess that the LORD is God in heaven and on earth. Hebrews 11:31 draws the same line: by faith she “did not perish with those who were disobedient.”

sides.label: Hears, and confesses the LORD
sides.words: for the LORD your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below

sides.who: all who dwell in the land
sides.label: Hear the same news, and lose heart
sides.words: all who dwell in the land are melting in fear of you

notes.evidence: T. E. Espin (Barnes' Notes): the same reports that brought the woman to faith brought only terror to her countrymen. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch): the wonders that led her to faith left the rest of the Canaanites hardened. Robert Jamieson (JFB): her words show the Canaanites' panic and her strong conviction. Clarke: she probably made better use of the light she had than the rest of her countrymen.
notes.limit: Rahab says that her own heart melted too. What sets her apart is not that she felt no fear, but that she believed what she heard and acted on it.

cites.quote: Rahab had only heard of what Israel had experienced. Her faith then was ready. It is noteworthy, too, that the same reports which work faith and conversion in the harlot, cause only terror and astonishment among her countrymen.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: But these miracles of divine omnipotence which led the heart of this sinner with its susceptibility for religious truth to true faith, and thus became to her a savour of life unto life, produced nothing but hardness in the unbelieving hearts of the rest of the Canaanites, so that they could not escape the judgment of death.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Rahab's dialogue is full of interest, as showing the universal panic and consternation of the Canaanites on the one hand ... and her strong convictions on the other
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: She probably made a better use of the light she had received than the rest of her countrymen, and God increased that light.

notes.short: “And” after “and”: all that was taken with Achan
notes.about: The verse names one by one all that was taken with Achan: the silver, the cloak, the gold, his sons and daughters, his animals, his tent and all he owned. In Hebrew each is joined by “and”, so each is weighed on its own, showing how solemn the judgment was and how great his sin.

figure.name: Polysyndeton
figure.words: the silver, the cloak, the bar of gold, his sons and daughters, his oxen and donkeys and sheep, his tent, and everything else he owned
figure.means: each thing taken with Achan, weighed on its own, showing how solemn the judgment was and how great his sin

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Polysyndeton: the conjunction comes again and again to show how solemn the judgment on Achan was and how great his sin. The BSB keeps only some of the ands; in the Hebrew every item is joined to the one before.

cites.quote: to show the awful solemnity of the judgment executed upon Achan, and the magnitude of his sin

notes.short: “Son of Zerah”: son put for a later descendant
notes.about: Achan is called the son of Zerah, yet verse 1 traces him through Carmi and Zabdi back to Zerah. Here “son” is put for a descendant further down the line, one relationship standing for another.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.part: of the Species: one relationship put for others
figure.means: a descendant of Zerah, not his own son: verse 1 names Carmi and Zabdi between them

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Species, where one relationship is put for others: Achan is called the son of Zerah, which stands for his great-grandson, as verse 1 shows.
notes.limit: Verse 1 names Carmi and Zabdi between Zerah and Achan. The note claims only that son here stands for a later descendant, not how many generations lie between them.

cites.quote: Achan is called “the son of Zerah,” which is put for great grandson.

notes.short: Joshua cries out in grief after the defeat at Ai
notes.about: After Israel's defeat at Ai, Joshua's prayer opens with a cry, “O, Lord GOD,” where a plain statement might stand. It voices his grief and distress to the LORD: why bring this people over the Jordan only to see them destroyed?

figure.name: Exclamation
figure.means: grief and distress cried out to God after Israel was routed at Ai

original.note: In Hebrew the cry opens with ahah, “alas”, a word of distress, which the BSB gives as “O”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Ecphonesis, an outburst of emotion. Clarke calls ahah, alas, a particle of exclamation and distress. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says they lay before the ark to pour out their grief, and calls the complaint faith wrestling with God; Jamieson (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls the prayer the effusion of an afflicted mind; Henry says he gave vent to his trouble.
notes.limit: The writers weigh the cry differently: it can be heard as a fretful complaint that doubts God, partly excused by his concern for Israel, or as bold faith pleading with God and caring for His honour.

cites.quote: The figure is used when, through feeling, we change our mode of speech; and, instead of merely making a statement, express it by an exclamation. So that Ecphonesis is an outburst of words, prompted by emotion, and is not used as though any reply were expected ... Alas, O Lord God (Adonai Jehovah), wherefore hast thou at all brought up this people over Jordan
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Particles of exclamations and distress, or what are called interjections, are nearly the same in all languages: and the reason is because they are the simple voice of nature. The Hebrew word which we translate alas is אהה ahah. The complaint of Joshua in this and the following verses seems principally to have arisen from his deep concern for the glory of God
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: In the deepest grief, with their clothes rent ... they fell down before the ark of the Lord ... until the evening, to pour out their grief before the Lord. Joshua's prayer contains a complaint ... it by no means arose from unbelief, but was simply the bold language of faith wrestling with God in prayer
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: although apparently breathing a spirit of bold remonstrance and complaint, it was in reality the effusion of a deeply humbled and afflicted mind
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: his spirit seemed to be somewhat ruffled and discomposed ... by giving vent to his trouble in a humble address to God, he keeps his temper and it ends well ... This savours too much of discontent and distrust of God, and cannot be justified, though the surprise and disappointment to one deeply concerned for the public interest may in part excuse it.

notes.short: Question and sentence, then answer and yielding
notes.about: Joshua asks why the Gibeonites deceived Israel and then pronounces their sentence. Their reply follows the same order: first the answer to his question, then their yielding to the sentence.

lines.words: Now therefore you are under a curse
Now we are in your hands.

notes.evidence: Boys sets the four verses out in four members that take turns: Joshua's question in the first is answered in the third, and the Gibeonites express submission in the fourth to the sentence he pronounces in the second.

cites.quote: In a. and b. we have the speech of Joshua; in a. and b., the reply of the Gibeonites. The point now to be established is, that the part of the reply in a. answers to the part of the speech in a.; and the part in b., to the part in b. … The Gibeonites reply to the question in a., and express submission to the sentence in b.
cites.read: the 1825 printing, in the scan at archive.org/details/akeytobookpsalm00boysgoog

notes.about: Balak sets out to fight Israel and sends for Balaam. The LORD would not listen to Balaam, and He delivered Israel from his hand. That hand is taken to be Balak's, so the first and last lines are both about Balak.

lines.words: Then Balak son of Zippor, the king of Moab, set out to fight against Israel.
He sent for Balaam son of Beor to curse you,
but I would not listen to Balaam.
and I delivered you from his hand.

notes.evidence: Boys sets the two verses out in four lines and says the hand the LORD delivered Israel from is Balak's, not Balaam's: the first and last lines refer to Balak, the two between to Balaam.

cites.quote: The person, however, out of whose hand the Lord, in a., says he delivered the Israelites, is not Balaam, but Balak, mentioned in a. … Thus a. and a. refer to Balak; b. and b. to Balaam.
